one_liner: Objeck: object-oriented language with a C++ VM and AMD64/ARM64 method JIT; beats CPython and Ruby, LuaJIT only on binarytrees.
what_it_does: A self-contained statically typed object-oriented and functional language: obc compiles .obs source to bytecode, obr runs it in a C++ stack VM that JIT-compiles hot methods to x64 or ARM64. It is a separate language with a large standard library (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, JSON, ONNX/OpenCV bindings, an ML package), not a drop-in for Lua, Python or Java code.
how_it_is_fast: A single-pass method JIT translates each method's bytecode with an accumulator model, keeps locals in native stack slots with a register cache, folds constants and strength-reduces division, and emits inline nil, bounds and divide-by-zero checks. Methods marked native are always compiled and other methods auto-JIT after 10 calls; since v2026.9.1 compiled callers enter compiled callees directly through a native calling convention with inline caches at virtual and function-reference sites. A young-generation bump allocator with parallel marking is what took binarytrees from 8.53 s to 2.14 s.
when_to_use: You want a small batteries-included OO scripting language that runs integer and call-heavy code 13-47x faster than CPython 3.12 and Ruby 3.2 (nbody, spectralnorm, fannkuchredux rows of the Docker run).
Allocation-heavy tree code where it measured 2.14 s against LuaJIT 2.1's 3.57 s and CPython's 3.48 s on binarytrees depth 17, if 209 MB peak RSS is acceptable.
Projects that would otherwise glue a scripting language to HTTP/3, ONNX or OpenCV libraries and value having those in the standard library on Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and ARM64.
when_not_to_use: Float-heavy loops: nbody is 1.9x slower than LuaJIT and 3.5x slower than OpenJDK 21, spectralnorm about 2.4x slower than both.
When Java, .NET or Julia is an option: HotSpot won 3 of the 4 cross-language rows (binarytrees 8.2x faster than Objeck), even running the naive fannkuchredux port.
Code that relies on Try() for error recovery in hot paths: methods holding a Try region never JIT, and issue #925 (errors raised inside JIT-compiled code cannot be caught by Try()) is still open.

Production systems that need a long-stable compiler: the September-October 2026 releases fixed several silent miscompiles at the default -opt s3 level (#1037 infinite loop from inlined helpers, #988 Bool[] call results), NaN comparisons that were all true on Windows (#1000) and GC/thread crashes (#874, #877, #913).

integration.form: language toolchain (obc compiler and obr VM binaries; release archives for Windows, Linux and macOS)
integration.dependencies: Linux release needs system mbedTLS, readline, SDL2/GL, OpenCV, unixODBC and LAME (install_deps.sh); a source-built obr links mbedTLS and zlib plus static nghttp2, ngtcp2, nghttp3 and AWS-LC built by tools/deps/build_quic_deps.sh
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows on x86-64 and ARM64 (JIT on both); the stock amd64 source build uses -mavx2 so needs an AVX2 CPU
integration.thread_safety: Language-level threads with a parallel-marking GC; several thread/GC races were fixed in September 2026 (#874, #877, #913); embedding thread rules not documented

gotchas: Harness flaw: every benchmark's output goes to /dev/null unchecked and the cross-language runner discards stderr (eval "$cmd" > /dev/null 2>&1), so a crashed or miscompiled run would still be timed; the page itself says this hid a fasta compile failure and a Console->WriteBuffer double-encoding bug for months, and v2026.10.0 later fixed an -opt s3 miscompile (#1037) in the same optimizer level the benchmarks used.

The 3.6x fannkuchredux win over LuaJIT compares Objeck's optimized CLBG algorithm (native-annotated, reversal of the inner span only) with a naive Lua port that allocates and fills a fresh table per permutation; it measures the Lua program, not LuaJIT.

The JIT does no inlining (ProcessInlineMethod is never called, yet every compiled frame reserves inline stack space), methods with frame-dependent traps (serialization, time, file-time calls) stay interpreted, and on ARM64 an expression with more than twelve live temporaries falls back to the interpreter whole.

Timings come from Docker on a Windows 11 host, where the page says interpreter-bound rows run 30-50% slower than native, and LuaJIT, Python, Ruby and Java are Ubuntu 24.04 apt packages with unrecorded builds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Objeck over WrenJIT or stryke when you want a full general-purpose language with a mature standard library rather than a single fast embeddable VM; for raw throughput against LuaJIT the .NET runtime, Julia, Dart or Chez Scheme entries beat it on independent shootouts, and Objeck's own table shows HotSpot ahead on 3 of 4 rows.
verified_claims_summary: In one Docker run (Ubuntu 24.04 on a Windows 11 host, Ryzen 9 7950X3D, median of 3), Objeck v2026.9.1 built with g++ -O3 -flto -mavx2 and programs compiled at -opt s3 ran binarytrees 17 in 2.14 s against LuaJIT 2.1's 3.57 s (1.7x, comparable single-threaded programs) but lost to LuaJIT on nbody (8.14 s vs 4.37 s) and spectralnorm (2.72 s vs 1.12 s); its fannkuchredux win (32.76 s vs 117.99 s) uses a weaker Lua program, and OpenJDK 21 beat Objeck on nbody, binarytrees and fannkuchredux.
status_note: Very active (releases every few weeks, v2026.9.7 current with v2026.10.0 notes landed, last commit 2026-10-05) and BSD-3-Clause, but recent releases still fix silent miscompiles and GC races, so pin a release and run your own output checks.
